4. Mr. MI Farooqui, appearing on behalf of the opposite party, opposes the Rule on the ground that the forum of appeal at the relevant time was the High Court Division inasmuch as the appeal arises out of a suit valued at Tk. 48,000'00, whether the appeal is from a decree or from an order. In support of his contention he cites the decisions in the case of Colonial Sugar Refining Company Ltd. Vs. Irving, (1905) AC 369; the case of Venugopala Reddiar and another Vs. Krishnaswami Reddiar alias Raja Chidizmbara Reddiar and another 1943 (FC) 24 and the case of Bangladesh Vs. Shahjahan Siraj@ Sirajul Islam, 32 DLR (AD) 1. Mr. Farooqui also referred me to section 6(e) of the General Clauses Act to argue that the forum of appeal, the High Court Division, is protected in spite of the amendment brought by the Amending Ordinance No. II of 1983 in the present case. The decision in the case of Colonial Sugar Refining Company Ltd. was considered in Mozaffar Ahmed wherein the point mooted before me was the same. In Mozaffar Ahmed the question relates to the interpretation of section 21 of the Bengal Civil Courts Act, 1887 as amended by section 3 of the East Pakistan Act. No. 1 of 1964 which came into force on January 25, 1964. 

 "Notwithstanding anything contained in section 21 of the said Act, as amended by section 3 of this Act, any appeal from a decree or order of a Civil Court subordinate to the court of a District Judge, which, immediately before the commencement of this Act, was pending before a High Court or District Judge shall be proceeded with and heard and disposed of by the High Court or the District Judge, as the case may be, as if this Act had not been passed." 

 "The appeals in such cases in which decrees are passed on or after the 25th of January, 1964, must lie to the District Judge." 

 "21 (1) Save as aforesaid, an appeal from a decree or order of a subordinate Judge shall lie. 

 (a) to the District Judge where the value of the original suit in which or in any proceeding arising out of which the decree or order was made did not exceed twenty thousand rupees, and 

 A plain reading of the amended section 21 of the Act in an unambiguous language indicates that shall lie to the District Judge where the appeal is valued upto Tk. 70,000'00 although at the time of filing the suit the forum of appeal was not the District Judge in view of his pecuniary jurisdiction and the forum was the High Court Division. Section an appeal from the decree or order of the trial Court 5 of the amending Ordinance makes this point more clear. It says that the amendment shall not affect any suit or appeal or other proceeding pending in or before any court immediately before the commencement of the Ordinance and any such suit, appeal or proceeding shall continue and be disposed of as if the Ordinance had not come into force. Thus, reading sections 3 and 5 of the amending Ordinance together my irresistible conclusion is that the makers of the law had the clear intention that the appellate forum is the District Judge and the provision of section 5 only saves a pending suit, appeal or other proceedings in any court. 

 7. In this case when the appeal was preferred the amending Ordinance already came into force on January, 24, 1983 vesting the jurisdiction to District Judge to entertain and hear an appeal valued up to Tk. 70,000/-. The law that determines the forum of appeal is the law that is in existence at the time of 	filing the appeal and not the law that was in existence at the time of institution of the suit inasmuch as the right of appeal accrues only after the decree is made or the appellate order is passed in the suit, as in the present case. In the present case when the right of appeal accrued the forum was the District Judge. It is profitable in this respect to quote the learned Chief Justice" mere filing of a suit does not, by itself, clothe a suitor with any "vested right" in any particular kind of appeal. It is true and we may say so with respect that it is correct to say that at the time when a suit is brought, a chain of system including a process of appeal is set into motion which can be treated as a unit. But until the suit has fructified into a decree, no right of appeal is " vested" in any party to the suit. There may be an inchoate right of appeal in embryo; but until a decree is passed, no right has been born in the sense that the party has not yet been "vested" with any "right." This point already thus having been settled in Mozaffar Ahmed I am not inclined to discuss the decisions cited by Mr. Farooqui more so when the facts of those cases are distinguishable from the facts of the present case. It is true that section 3 of the present amending Ordinance No. II of 1983 is not retrospective in effect but that has not made the' Petitioner appeal incompetent before the District Judge inasmuch as at the time of filing the appeal the appellate forum was changed from that of the High Court Division to the District Judge.
